questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend building a single table that puts the base case and all stress tests side by side, rather than separate outputs for each?
options: Because pandas cannot display more than one result at a time
So a reviewer can compare every scenario across every metric at a glance, without hunting through separate code outputs — a habit that signals internalized Chapter 4/5 discipline
Because stress test results should never be shown alongside the base case
Tables are only useful for the base case; stress tests should be described in prose only
questions.explain: A single comparison table makes it impossible to misread or bury unfavorable stress-test results next to the base case, which the lesson identifies as a clear marker of a researcher who has genuinely internalized the course's realism and statistical-honesty lessons.

questions.q: According to the lesson's recommended write-up structure, what should come before the base case results section?
options: Nothing; the headline Sharpe ratio should always be the very first thing presented
The idea and five-component specification, followed by data and methodology, including what the backtest does NOT account for
A list of every other strategy that was tried and discarded, in full code
The interview talking points section
questions.explain: The recommended order is: idea and specification, then data and methodology (explicitly including what isn't accounted for), then base case results — deliberately not leading with the headline Sharpe ratio.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the strongest way to talk about this capstone in an interview, even if the strategy didn't survive stress-testing?
options: Omitting the stress test results entirely and only discussing the favorable base case

Walking through the process — specification, assumptions, what the stress tests probed, and what the result implied — since clearly explaining why a strategy failed demonstrates real research discipline
Claiming the strategy had a great Sharpe ratio regardless of the stress test outcomes
Refusing to discuss capstone results in interviews at all
questions.explain: The lesson argues that most candidates can show an inflated, unstressed Sharpe ratio, but few can clearly explain why a strategy failed a stress test and what they'd try next — making that explanation the genuinely strong answer.

questions.q: What four things does the lesson recommend disclosing explicitly in any published write-up of this capstone?
options: Only the final Sharpe ratio, rounded to one decimal place

The exact sample period and length, every cost/fill assumption, the number of variants tried before settling on the presented one, and a clear statement that it isn't investment advice or a live track record
The strategy's source code only, with no narrative explanation
A guarantee of future performance based on the backtest
questions.explain: The lesson lists these specific disclosures — sample period, explicit assumptions, number of variants tried (tying back to Lesson 19's data-snooping honesty), and a clear non-advice disclaimer — as costing nothing in credibility while actually building it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a strategy that "didn't survive its own stress tests, explained clearly" can be a stronger portfolio piece than an unstressed, flattering result?
options: Because failed strategies are inherently more interesting to read about
Because it demonstrates the actual research discipline the course taught — honest methodology and stress-testing — rather than just the ability to produce one favorable number
Because reviewers always prefer negative results over positive ones
Because an unstressed result is always mathematically incorrect
questions.explain: The lesson's consistent theme is that the skill being demonstrated is the research process itself — honest methodology, realistic assumptions, and genuine stress-testing — not the ability to manufacture an impressive-looking number, which is why a well-explained negative result reflects stronger work.
